assumptions: Atmosphere is a single layer of air at temperature T_a
Atmosphere is completely transparent to shortwave solar radiation.
Atmosphere is completely opaque to infrared radiation
Both surface and atmosphere emit radiation as blackbodies (σT_s⁴, σT_a⁴)
Atmosphere radiates equally up and down (σT_a⁴)
There are no other heat transfer mechanisms
greenhouse.result: Solve for the surface temperature: T_s = 2^(1/4) T_e
greenhouse.example: Putting in observed numbers, T_e = 255 K gives a surface temperature of T_s = 303 K
greenhouse.over: Our model now overpredicts the surface temperature by about 15ºC (303 K versus the observed 288 K).
reasons: Atmosphere is NOT a perfect absorber of longwave radiation
Energy is redistributed in the vertical by a variety of dynamical transport mechanisms (e.g. convection and boundary layer turbulence).
greenhouse.grey: This is called the grey gas model, where grey here means the emission and absorption have no spectral dependence (same at every wavelength).
greenhouse.layers: Suppose that we pile on another perfectly absorbing layer on top of the one that we've already considered. Using the short cut we infer that the radiation emitted from the top layer of the atmosphere must still be E; the radiation emitted upward from the bottom layer of the atmosphere must be equal to 2E and the radiation emitted from the surface must be 3E. It's not difficult to extend this simple analysis to additional layers.
greenhouse.convection: Conduction of heat and evaporation of water transfer about twice as much energy from the earth's surface to the atmosphere as the net upward flux of infrared radiation from the radiation does. If the temperature distribution on earth were determined only by radiative transfer (as in this example) the earth would be so hot as to be uninhabitable.
greenhouse.extension: N layers → the surface emits (N + 1)E, so T_s = (N + 1)^¼ T_e: our extension of the printed 2E and 3E pattern.

insolation.eq: Q̄^day = (S_0/π) (d̄/d)² ( h_0 sin φ sin δ + cos φ cos δ sin h_0 )
insolation.h0: Sunrise and sunset occur when the solar zenith angle is 90º and thus cos θ_s = 0. The above formula then gives cos h_0 = − tan φ tan δ where h_0 is the hour angle at sunrise and sunset.
insolation.decl: the latitude of the point on the surface of Earth directly under the sun at noon (denoted by δ). δ currenly varies between +23.45º at northern summer solstice (June 21) to -23.45º at northern winter solstice (Dec. 21).
insolation.polarDay: Latitudes poleward of 90º- δ are constantly illuminated in summer, when φ and δ are of the same sign.
insolation.polarNight: In the winter, φ and δ are of opposite sign, and latitudes poleward of 90º- |δ| are in perpetual darkness.
insolation.clamp: Where −tan φ tan δ < −1 (polar day) we take h₀ = π, and where it exceeds +1 (polar night) h₀ = 0 — the formula form of the two quoted statements.

nasa.q: Hurricanes form over tropical waters (between 8 and 20 degrees latitude) in areas of high humidity, light winds, and warm sea surface temperatures [typically 26.5 degrees Celsius (80 Fahrenheit) or greater].

nps.q: Sea temperatures of at least 80°F (26.5°C) are required to spawn hurricanes.

gfdl.q: For hurricane wind speeds, our model shows a sensitivity of about 4% per degree Celsius increase in tropical sea surface temperatures, with a larger percentage increase in near-storm rainfall.

gfdl2.q: Tropical cyclone intensities globally are projected to increase ( medium to high confidence ) on average (by 1 to 10% according to model projections for a 2 degree Celsius global warming).

cyclone.bases: GFDL’s “about 4% per degree Celsius” is per °C of tropical sea-surface temperature in one early model study; its “1 to 10%” is per 2 °C of global warming. Different bases — not combined here.

jotr.q: The area of southeastern California is a rain shadow desert. The rain shadow effect is produced by the high mountains on the west, which block the movement of wet winter storms. As coastal storms move in from the west they collide with Mount San Jacinto (10,804 ft.) and Mount San Gorgonio (11,502 ft.). The air rises, cools, and precipitation falls on the mountains.

olympic.q: By the time any storm cells pass the Olympic Mountains, most of the moisture has been released. … Located in Port Angeles, the Olympic National Park Headquarters only averages 25-30 inches a year.

brochure.q: the mountains force clouds upward. As the air gets colder and air pressure decreases, these storm clouds cannot hold as much moisture and the water falls as rain in the lowlands and snow in the high country.

rotation.rossby: This can be quantified by the Rossby number, Ro = U/fL, defined as the ratio between advection forces and Coriolis forces in the horizontal momentum equation.
rotation.slow: terrestrial planets with rotation periods longer than ∼10 Earth days may represent "all tropics" worlds
rotation.venusTitan: Venus and Titan are examples in our own solar system, exhibiting near-global Hadley cells, minimal equator-pole temperature differences, little role for baroclinic instabilities, and a zonal jet structure that differs significantly from those on Earth and Mars.
rotation.fast: a case at four times the Earth rotation rate … the deformation radius is four times smaller, and the baroclinic zone breaks up into three jets in each hemisphere.
rotation.large: When a planet is small, like Earth or Mars, only one strip of baroclinic instabilities—and one eddy-driven jet—can fit into the baroclinic zone … When the planet is relatively large relative to the eddy size, however, the baroclinic zone breaks up into multiple bands of baroclinic instability, and hence multiple jet streams.
rotation.trend: At slow rotation rates, the Hadley cells are nearly global, the subtropical jets reside at high latitude, and the equator-pole temperature difference is small. … At faster rotation rates, the Hadley cells and subtropical jets contract toward the equator, an extratropical zone, with eddy-driven jets, develops at high latitudes, and the equator-pole temperature difference is large.

titan.q: Such a large Hadley cell is only possible on a slowly rotating world, such as Titan where one day equals 16 Earth days.

jupiter.q: Jupiter's fast rotation – spinning once every 10 hours – creates strong jet streams, separating its clouds into dark belts and bright zones across long stretches.

titan.synchronous: S indicates synchronous rotation - the rotation period is the same as the orbital period
titan.geomNote: NSSDCA’s 0.22 for Titan is a “Visual geometric albedo”, not the Bond albedo the energy balance needs.
